extracted.intended_audience: instructors/instructional designers of online team learning modules and online learners/participants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for designing, facilitating, and participating in team-based online learning and project work, including chat protocols, team-charter development, role assignment, progress monitoring, and socialization practices. Emphasizes experiential (tacit) and explicit learning, trust building, and appropriate use of communication tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chat communication etiquette / signalling
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of explicit chat-room conventions for signalling completion, confusion, reactions, and behaviour in synchronous text sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original guidance includes: "Signal when you’ve finished a statement [some use a happy face to signal they have completed their input]. Signal when you don’t understand something; use a question mark to get the facilitator’s attention. Signal your 'reactions' by using an exclamation mark (!) for surprise, a sad face for disagreement, or some combination of symbols. Do not shout [CAPITALS MEAN THAT YOU ARE SHOUTING]. Do not leave your computer during a scheduled session; it is impossible to get your attention if you leave the room. Officially sign on and off so that everyone knows when you are present. Keep statements brief and to the point; the chat box has a limit of 256 characters per statement; you can keep talking, but in spurts. Prepare notes and key ideas ahead of time so that you can engage in the discussion without trying to figure out how to word your statements. (CPLI, 2000, p. 45)"

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish team-charter template (ground rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a team-charter template that serves as a checklist and governing tool for team work and social interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The completed team-charter "resembles a checklist, and represents the collective wisdom of what the team members believe to be the important issues to be addressed in creating and deploying an effective team as quickly as possible." It should contain ideas on how teams should be formed and structured; how their purpose should be defined; how team culture should be developed; and how the team should collaborate, ensure accountability, measure success, and achieve high performance. Learners first respond individually to questions and then synthesize into one common document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign and rotate roles (leader, scribe, timekeeper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteer for specific roles and rotate them among participants to allow for skill development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members volunteer for roles of leader, scribe, and timekeeper – roles that are rotated among participants, to allow for skill development. Role rotation supports learning and distributes responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitator use of constraints to provoke learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitator deliberately introduces new constraints and surprises to surface differences and provoke conflict for experiential learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The facilitator introduces constraints such as transport route changes, modes of transportation, environmental conditions, presence of wildlife, hazardous goods handling, etc., to "force differences among team members to the surface" so participants can experience and work through conflict and develop competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize consensus as the decision rule for the team task to ensure full participation and shared ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitators emphasize the importance of consensus decision making for the task; team discussions may reveal differing views (e.g., "troublemakers had the option to leave the team" vs. "consensus must occur"), and facilitators can use such teachable moments to link discussion with lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare concise contributions and notes ahead of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should prepare notes and key ideas in advance and keep chat contributions brief and to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: "Prepare notes and key ideas ahead of time so that you can engage in the discussion without trying to figure out how to word your statements." Also: "Keep statements brief and to the point; the chat box has a limit of 256 characters per statement; you can keep talking, but in spurts."

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance and presence protocol (sign on/off; remain present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish clear sign-on/sign-off procedures and require participants to remain present during scheduled synchronous sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Officially sign on and off so that everyone knows when you are present." Also: "Do not leave your computer during a scheduled session; it is impossible to get your attention if you leave the room." These conventions ensure accountability and awareness of presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match communication medium to task
rubrics_metrics.description: Use different communication tools for different purposes—chat for planning/decisions, email/message boards for in-depth work, conference calls for richer interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from practice: teams often used email and the message board for in-depth communications, and the chat tool for work planning or coming to final decisions. Conference calls and face-to-face events were used for social history and richer discussion. Align the medium (asynchronous vs synchronous) with task needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement on team working principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams should come to explicit or emergent agreements about how they will work together, including expectations for deadlines, leadership, contribution, and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative emergent principles from a successful research team: "The deadlines must be met." "Whoever was best able to lead on a particular task would do so." "Each member would contribute 150% to this project"; "Team members would raise a flag (let others know about tasks not likely to get done on time)." "Team members would pitch in to complete work as needed." These principles helped monitor alignment with overall goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of accountability while building flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Define accountability and roles clearly, but allow flexibility so members can take responsibility based on availability/expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Header: "Assignment of Accountability and Building in Flexibility." Guidance notes: clearly defined roles are essential, but online teams require flexibility; leadership may shift; sometimes initial responsibility is assigned and then traded off as necessary. Careful record keeping and tracking help manage ambiguous roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use project-management practices for project work
rubrics_metrics.description: When the task is project-based, explicitly apply project-management practices: define deliverables, deadlines, tracking, and formal reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case contrast: the research project team explicitly recognized activities as a project and engaged in good project management practices, including deadlines, leads on tasks, and formal monthly status reports to sponsors. MBA teams often viewed work as process/grade-driven and less likely to use formal project management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring progress regularly (meetings, minutes, reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement regular progress-monitoring mechanisms—conference calls, minutes, status reports, and scheduled chats—to check social, project, and external activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the research team used weekly one-hour conference calls structured as: first five minutes social history, ~45 minutes detailed discussion of deliverables/status, final 10 minutes report external commitments. They also submitted monthly status reports to the sponsor. The TDC module used weekly scheduled chats to structure progress monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate social interaction and celebration
rubrics_metrics.description: Build social interaction and fun into project routines to sustain motivation, trust, and camaraderie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific practices: "Celebrate success" (kudos at start of calls, e-cards), "Plan for interaction" (set aside funds/time for face-to-face or celebratory events), and "Communicate about other than project activities" (catch up on personal lives). Provide informal 'water cooler' spaces (non-graded workspaces) to share humour and life events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create kick-off events to establish rapport
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an initial event (face-to-face, voice, or structured online) to establish bonds and make shifting roles more comfortable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature suggests a need for some form of 'kick-off event' for online teams. Face-to-face may be superior, but voice and online alternatives also work; prior face-to-face or an initial bonding event helps when roles shift and ambiguity arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build trust in technology, process, and each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly cultivate trust in the communication medium, the facilitation process, and among team members to enable effective collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed outcomes: after initial chat experiences, participants became comfortable with the technologically mediated environment and one another. Trust increased with repeated interaction and led to tacit use of technology, self-organization, and better collaboration. Trust is supported via effective leadership, tools (team charters/chat protocols), and predictable processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage explicit and tacit learning; leverage teachable moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Design activities that produce both explicit discussion of concepts and tacit experiential learning; highlight teachable moments when process parallels content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a heated discussion about conflict resolution became a teachable moment when participants recognized that the discussion mirrored the topic, combining intellectual and experiential elements. The team-charter task provided opportunity to crystallize learning in a tangible document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal management and interpersonal competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster individual capabilities such as prioritization, limit-setting, feedback exchange, boundary management, and cultural awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational factors, technology use, personal management, and interpersonal skills are important. Personal management includes ability to prioritize work, set limits, create opportunities for learning and growth, collect and provide feedback, discuss strengths and weaknesses, manage boundaries, and understand cultural perspectives and how differences affect perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share personal schedules and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Team members should disclose schedules and availability so work can be coordinated given temporal and geographic differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical example: team members shared that one worked early/late, another was a night owl, others had flexible daytime hours; members picked up and organized work after another stopped to enable continuous progress. Sharing availability improves coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice self-monitoring and proactive communication to avoid free-riding
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals must self-monitor, monitor team processes, and proactively communicate problems to prevent free-loader behaviour and maintain commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The balance between accountability and flexibility requires self-monitoring and proactive commitment. Those whose goal is merely course completion are more likely to free-load. Open communication of goals and expectations, status reporting, and process feedback help mitigate disparities.
